title: DriftSR: One-Step Real-World Image Super-Resolution via Distribution Drifting

paper.title: DriftSR: One-Step Real-World Image Super-Resolution via Distribution Drifting
paper.abstract: Abstract One-step real-world image super-resolution (Real-ISR) offers efficient inference, but recovering realistic and perceptually rich details often relies on score distillation or adversarial learning, introducing additional trainable components and making optimization more cumbersome. To this end, we propose DriftSR, a one-step Real-ISR framework that leverages pretrained diffusion priors through distribution drifting. Specifically, we perform drifting in the frozen intermediate representation space of a pretrained diffusion model, without introducing an additional task-specific feature encoder. Building on this space, we introduce Spatial Feature Drifting, which treats spatial features rather than entire images as distributional samples, enabling denser supervision for distribution alignment. To mitigate structural deviations, we further introduce Structure-Modulated Guidance, which adaptively refines drifting guidance according to local structural consistency with the LQ input. Consequently, DriftSR optimizes only the one-step generator, without auxiliary distillation branches or adversarial discriminators. Extensive experiments on three real-world benchmarks demonstrate that DriftSR delivers high-quality super-resolution reconstruction with efficient one-step inference.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Real-world image super-resolution (Real-ISR) [ 46 , 32 , 48 , 47 , 51 ] aims to recover high-quality (HQ) images from low-quality (LQ) observations affected by unknown and complex degradations. The mapping from LQ observations to HQ images is inherently ambiguous, and pixel-level reconstruction objectives often lead to over-smoothed results [ 17 , 24 ] . Therefore, recovering natural image details while maintaining content and structural fidelity to the input remains a central challenge in Real-ISR [ 37 , 29 ] . Recently, large-scale pretrained diffusion models have significantly advanced Real-ISR by providing strong generative priors for natural images [ 29 , 43 , 39 , 10 ] . As the field shifts from iterative diffusion-based restoration toward efficient one-step generation, a key challenge is to recover realistic and perceptually rich details within a single forward pass. To address this challenge, existing diffusion-based one-step SR methods [ 37 , 30 , 45 , 18 ] often employ score distillation or adversarial learning to enhance perceptual details. Score distillation approaches [ 33 , 37 , 10 ] typically rely on an additional teacher model and trainable LoRA branches, with the LoRA parameters optimized under diffusion-based supervision throughout training. Adversarial approaches [ 13 , 45 , 18 ] instead introduce an additional discriminator and may suffer from unstable optimization. Despite their effectiveness in improving perceptual quality, both paradigms require auxiliary trainable components and additional objectives, increasing the complexity of the training pipeline. This motivates a simpler alternative that optimizes only the one-step generator while effectively leveraging generative priors. The recently proposed Drifting Model [ 8 ] introduces an alternative to score distillation and adversarial learning for distributional generative optimization. It models the relation between source and target distributions in a pretrained feature space and constructs a drifting field guiding generated samples toward the target distribution. By operating on sample distributions without an additional discriminator or a separately optimized distillation branch, distribution drifting presents a potential alternative for one-step Real-ISR. Nevertheless, directly extending distribution drifting to one-step Real-ISR is non-trivial. First , the effectiveness of the drifting field depends strongly on the feature space used to measure sample relationships, while obtaining a suitable representation may require additional design for Real-ISR. Second , drifting at the image level constructs negative samples by excluding the current sample and therefore requires additional samples under the same condition. Such a requirement can be naturally satisfied in image generation conditioned on class labels or text prompts, where multiple images can share the same condition. In contrast, Real-ISR provides only one paired HQ target for each LQ input, leaving no additional sample for negative construction and thus preventing direct application of drifting at the image level. Third , Real-ISR requires both high perceptual quality and fidelity to the LQ input. Excessive drifting may encourage visually plausible textures that are inconsistent with the input, resulting in incorrect details and structural distortions. Figure 1 : Qualitative and quantitative comparison of different training objectives. Left : Reconstruction-only training with MSE and LPIPS produces over-smoothed results. Adding variational score distillation [ 33 ] improves perceptual details, while further incorporating the GAN objective from OMGSR [ 40 ] enhances texture realism at the cost of additional trainable components. Our drifting loss achieves comparable or better perceptual quality without introducing additional trainable modules. Right : MANIQA and MUSIQ scores on four real-world datasets, where drifting remains competitive with joint score distillation and adversarial training. To address these challenges, we propose DriftSR , a one-step Real-ISR framework that adapts distribution drifting for perceptual detail enhancement. Inspired by Teacher-Feature Drifting (TFD) [ 50 ] , we employ the pretrained diffusion model as a frozen feature extractor and construct the drifting space using its intermediate representations. This design eliminates the need for an additional task-specific feature network while providing a representation space naturally aligned with the diffusion prior used by the generator. We further introduce Spatial Feature Drifting , which reformulates distribution modeling from the image level to the spatial feature level. By treating each spatial location as an individual sample, this formulation enables negative sample construction within each image and provides denser observations for modeling local texture distributions. To balance perceptual enhancement and input fidelity, we propose Structure-Modulated Guidance . Based on local structural consistency with the LQ input, this guidance adaptively modulates drifting supervision across spatial locations, thereby suppressing visually plausible but structurally inconsistent details. As shown in Figure 1 , these designs collectively enable DriftSR to leverage the pretrained diffusion prior for perceptual detail enhancement while preserving structural fidelity, with optimization restricted to the one-step generator. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose DriftSR, a one-step Real-ISR framework that introduces Spatial Feature Drifting to model distributions over spatial features and enhance perceptual details without additional trainable components. • We introduce Structure-Modulated Guidance to adaptively modulate drifting supervision based on local structural consistency with the LQ input, suppressing structural inconsistencies while preserving perceptually rich textures. • Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks demonstrate that our DriftSR achieves superior perceptual quality while maintaining efficient one-step inference.

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: One-Step Diffusion-based Real-ISR. To reduce diffusion model inference costs in Real-ISR, recent studies have increasingly explored one-step generative models replacing iterative generation with a single forward pass [ 44 , 42 , 37 ] . These methods aim to substantially improve inference efficiency while preserving high perceptual restoration quality. Existing one-step Real-ISR methods [ 31 , 42 , 10 ] commonly adopt distribution or trajectory alignment objectives during training. Among them, distribution alignment is often achieved through score distillation, which constructs supervision from the score discrepancy between a frozen diffusion teacher and a trainable LoRA branch. Some methods further incorporate adversarial learning [ 45 , 18 , 52 ] to enhance perceptual quality, introducing an additional discriminator. Although these strategies achieve strong restoration performance, the auxiliary trainable components and additional objectives increase the complexity of the training pipeline. Therefore, we explore a simpler alternative that leverages pretrained diffusion priors to guide one-step Real-ISR, without auxiliary distillation branches or discriminators. Drifting Model. Drifting Model [ 8 ] introduces a new paradigm for one-step generation by moving distribution transport from inference to training. Unlike diffusion or flow-based models [ 23 , 12 , 3 ] that rely on iterative inference, the drifting model learns a one-step generator whose output distribution is progressively updated during training under a drifting field defined by a kernel. The drifting field attracts generated samples toward nearby target samples while repelling them from the current model distribution, thereby progressively aligning the two distributions. Since distribution transport is performed during training, inference requires only a single forward pass. The effectiveness of the drifting model depends on the representation space used to measure sample relationships [ 8 ] . For high-dimensional images, distances measured in pixel or latent space may not adequately capture perceptual and semantic similarity. The drifting model therefore uses pretrained representations to construct informative feature spaces, making the choice of feature space important for effective distribution alignment.

sections.heading: 3.3 Spatial Feature Drifting
sections.text: The effectiveness of distribution drifting depends strongly on the feature space used to measure sample similarity. Inspired by TFD [ 50 ] , we employ a frozen pretrained diffusion model as the feature extractor and construct the drifting field in its intermediate feature space. This design offers two advantages. First, it avoids the need for a handcrafted or separately trained feature extractor specifically tailored to Real-ISR. Second, the generator is initialized from the same pretrained diffusion model and therefore inherits a compatible representation hierarchy. This shared initialization naturally aligns the drifting feature space with the representations inherited by the generator, enabling more consistent measurement of sample similarity during optimization. Both images are first encoded into the latent space: z ^ = E ψ ​ ( x ^ H ) , z = E ψ ​ ( x H ) . \hat{z}=E_{\psi}(\hat{x}_{H}),\qquad z=E_{\psi}(x_{H}). Direct image-level drifting treats the representation of each image as a single sample, which limits its applicability to Real-ISR because each LQ input is associated with only one paired HQ reference during training. To overcome this limitation, we exploit the spatial structure preserved in the teacher features and treat spatial feature vectors as individual drifting samples. This spatial formulation converts each training pair into N ℓ N_{\ell} feature samples, allowing positive and negative sample sets to be constructed within a single pair. It also provides denser observations for distribution modeling and captures local feature variations that are important for perceptual restoration. V^{\ell}=V_{P^{\ell},Q^{\ell}}\left(Q^{\ell}\right). (13) By modeling distributions over spatial features rather than entire image representations, this formulation enables distribution drifting within each paired training example despite the limited number of image-level references.

When the reconstructed structure becomes less consistent with the LQ input than the HQ reference, the corresponding modulation coefficient decreases. Since G θ G_{\theta} starts directly from the LQ input without introducing noise corruption and is trained with reconstruction objectives, the overall content and coarse structure are largely preserved. However, the original drifting field may still introduce high-frequency details that are inconsistent with the input structure. To provide additional structural guidance, we construct a low-frequency drifting field that emphasizes coarse image content while reducing the influence of high-frequency details. Specifically, DWT is applied to x ^ H \hat{x}_{H} and x H x_{H} to obtain x ^ H low \hat{x}_{H}^{\mathrm{low}} and x H low x_{H}^{\mathrm{low}} . Finally, we incorporate the structure-modulated drifting field into a unified drifting objective and aggregate it over all selected teacher layers: ℒ drift = ∑ ℓ ∈ 𝒮 1 N ℓ ​ C ℓ ​ ‖ Q ℓ − sg ⁡ ( Q ℓ + V SMG ℓ ) ‖ 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{drift}}=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}}\frac{1}{N_{\ell}C_{\ell}}\left\|Q^{\ell}-\operatorname{sg}\left(Q^{\ell}+V_{\mathrm{SMG}}^{\ell}\right)\right\|^{2}. (20) This formulation adaptively balances perceptual detail refinement and structural guidance. By modulating the drifting direction before constructing the optimization target, SMG integrates perceptual enhancement and structural guidance within a single drifting objective. sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Settings
sections.text: Training and Evaluation Datasets. We train DriftSR on LSDIR [ 19 ] and construct synthetic LR-HR pairs using the Real-ESRGAN degradation pipeline [ 32 ] . Degradation-aware prompt extraction (DAPE) [ 39 ] is adopted to generate textual descriptions. For evaluation, we conduct experiments on three real-world benchmarks, including RealSR [ 5 ] , DRealSR [ 35 ] and RealLQ250 [ 1 ] . Implementation details are provided in the supplementary material . Compared Methods. We compare our method with state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods, including the one-step methods OSEDiff [ 37 ] , CTMSR [ 42 ] , PiSA-SR [ 27 ] , TSD-SR [ 10 ] , HYPIR [ 20 ] , VOSR [ 38 ] , FiDeSR [ 15 ] , and StrSR [ 30 ] , as well as the multi-step methods StableSR [ 29 ] , ResShift [ 44 ] , DiT4SR [ 11 ] , and SeeSR [ 39 ] . Specifically, DiT4SR and TSD-SR are both built on SD3.5-Medium [ 12 ] , whereas StrSR adopts FLUX.2-klein-4B [ 3 ] . ResShift, CTMSR, and VOSR are developed without T2I priors. Evaluation Metrics. We comprehensively evaluate all methods using both full-reference and no-reference metrics. Specifically, PSNR and SSIM [ 34 ] are used to measure reconstruction fidelity, while LPIPS [ 49 ] is used to assess perceptual similarity. For no-reference perceptual quality assessment, we report MUSIQ [ 14 ] , MANIQA [ 41 ] , CLIPIQA [ 28 ] , TOPIQ [ 6 ] , and QALIGN [ 36 ] . In particular, QALIGN leverages a large multimodal model for image quality assessment and exhibits stronger alignment with human perceptual judgments. sections.heading: 4.2 Comparison with State-of-the-Arts
sections.text: Quantitative Comparisons. Table 1 compares DriftSR with existing diffusion-based methods on three real-world datasets. The results yield three main observations. (1) DriftSR achieves the best overall performance on no-reference perceptual metrics across all three benchmarks. The advantage is particularly pronounced on the higher-resolution RealLQ250 dataset, indicating that DriftSR can more effectively leverage the rich generative priors of pretrained diffusion models to recover realistic perceptual details. (2) ResShift, CTMSR, and VOSR employ purely visual architectures without T2I diffusion priors. Although these methods achieve competitive performance on full-reference metrics such as PSNR and SSIM, they generally underperform DriftSR on no-reference perceptual metrics, suggesting limitations in recovering fine-grained high-frequency details. (3) Despite using the same SD2.1 prior, FiDeSR favors fidelity-oriented reconstruction, whereas DriftSR achieves substantially better perceptual performance, particularly on CLIPIQA and TOPIQ. Meanwhile, DriftSR does not consistently achieve the best scores on full-reference metrics, while maintaining strong perceptual performance. This observation is consistent with the recognized trade-off between fidelity and perceptual quality [ 4 , 9 ] . As richer perceptual details are recovered, full-reference metrics may not fully reflect perceptual quality and often favor smoother reconstructions [ 43 , 39 ] . Qualitative Comparisons. Figure 3 presents visual comparisons among different methods. In the first row, DriftSR reconstructs more natural and perceptually realistic textures, particularly for fine animal fur. Although ResShift, CTMSR, and VOSR achieve competitive PSNR and SSIM scores, their results exhibit noticeable over-smoothing. In the second row, DriftSR effectively suppresses degradation artifacts and recovers clearer structures with consistent colors, whereas other one-step methods show limited recovery of fine structures and fail to correct color distortions. These comparisons further demonstrate the stronger capability of DriftSR to leverage the generative prior. More visual comparisons are provided in the supplementary material . Complexity Comparisons. We further evaluate the computational efficiency of representative Real-ISR methods in Table 2 , considering inference steps, runtime, and model parameters. We measure inference time on the × 4 \times 4 SR task with 128 × 128 128\times 128 LQ inputs, applying bicubic upsampling before inference on a single NVIDIA 5880 GPU. DriftSR substantially reduces inference cost compared with multi-step methods. It is more than 72 times faster than StableSR, 35 times faster than DiT4SR, over 32 times faster than SeeSR, and 7 times faster than ResShift. Compared with existing one-step models, DriftSR matches OSEDiff in inference speed and is 6 times faster than CTMSR. Despite being slower than VOSR, TSD-SR, and FiDeSR, DriftSR achieves a favorable balance between computational efficiency and perceptual restoration quality.

We ablate the feature space used to compute the drifting loss by replacing the teacher representation with VGG [ 26 ] , DINOv2 [ 22 ] , and DINOv3-ConvNeXt [ 25 ] , with three layers selected for each variant. As shown in Table 4 , DINOv3-ConvNeXt provides strong perceptual representations but yields worse LPIPS scores of 0.4171 and 0.4222 on RealSR and DRealSR, respectively. Visual comparisons in Figure 4 also show larger structural deviations from the LQ input, suggesting that stronger semantic representations are not necessarily well aligned with the structural constraints of image restoration. In contrast, the teacher feature space consistently outperforms VGG and DINOv2 on perceptual metrics across both benchmarks, indicating that it provides a more suitable representation space for drifting and a better balance between perceptual quality and structural fidelity. Effect of Teacher Layer Configurations. We further ablate the teacher layers used to compute the Drifting loss in the U-Net of SD2.1-Base and the MMDiT of SD3.5-Medium, as shown in Figure 5 . We report LPIPS for the U-Net and MANIQA for the MMDiT, as these metrics exhibit clearer trends across layer configurations. For the U-Net, features from different stages operate at different spatial scales and encode distinct representations. As shown in Figure 5 (a), D i D_{i} and U i U_{i} denote the downsampling and upsampling blocks indexed by i i , respectively, while M M denotes the bottleneck block. Different combinations of three layers yield only minor performance variations. In contrast, the number of selected layers has a larger impact, as increasing the number from three to five degrades the performance of DriftSR. For the MMDiT backbone, all transformer blocks operate at the same spatial resolution and differ mainly in network depth. Prior work [ 16 ] has shown that intermediate DiT blocks can exhibit stronger representations of class semantics. We therefore further investigate layer selection in DriftSR. As shown in Figure 5 (b), including the intermediate Block 12 provides no performance benefit. Instead, the results suggest that performance is more sensitive to the number of selected layers. Drifting Loss Suppresses Checkerboard Artifacts. With the pretrained SD3.5-Medium prior, the patch tokenization in MMDiT may contribute to periodic checkerboard artifacts. As shown in Figure 6 (a), we visualize the restoration results and corresponding 2D Fourier spectra at different training steps. Combining reconstruction loss (Rec.) with TSD [ 10 ] produces persistent periodic structures in the frequency domain. Adding GAN [ 40 ] supervision gradually reduces these artifacts during training but does not prevent their emergence at early stages. In contrast, replacing TSD with our Drifting loss effectively suppresses dense periodic patterns throughout training. Using the autocorrelation formulation in OP4KSR [ 7 ] as a reference, we further compute the Periodic Peak Score, as shown in Figure 6 (b), which quantitatively confirms the suppression of periodic artifacts by the drifting loss. Details of the Periodic Peak Score computation are provided in the supplementary material .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we presented DriftSR, a one-step Real-ISR framework that exploits pretrained diffusion priors through distribution drifting, with only the one-step generator optimized during training. We introduced Spatial Feature Drifting, which reformulates distribution drifting at the spatial feature level by treating each spatial location as a distributional sample. We further introduced Structure-Modulated Guidance, which adaptively refines the drifting guidance based on local structural consistency with the LQ input. Extensive experiments on three real-world benchmarks demonstrate that DriftSR achieves strong perceptual quality with efficient one-step inference, demonstrating the effectiveness of distribution drifting for Real-ISR.

To this end, we propose DriftSR, a one-step Real-ISR framework that leverages pretrained diffusion priors through distribution drifting. Specifically, we perform drifting in the frozen intermediate representation space of a pretrained diffusion model, without introducing an additional task-specific feature encoder. Building on this space, we introduce Spatial Feature Drifting, which treats spatial features rather than entire images as distributional samples, enabling denser supervision for distribution alignment. Extensive experiments on three real-world benchmarks demonstrate that DriftSR delivers high-quality super-resolution reconstruction with efficient one-step inference. 1 Introduction Real-world image super-resolution (Real-ISR) [ 46 , 32 , 48 , 47 , 51 ] aims to recover high-quality (HQ) images from low-quality (LQ) observations affected by unknown and complex degradations. The mapping from LQ observations to HQ images is inherently ambiguous, and pixel-level reconstruction objectives often lead to over-smoothed results [ 17 , 24 ] . Therefore, recovering natural image details while maintaining content and structural fidelity to the input remains a central challenge in Real-ISR [ 37 , 29 ] . Recently, large-scale pretrained diffusion models have significantly advanced Real-ISR by providing strong generative priors for natural images [ 29 , 43 , 39 , 10 ] . As the field shifts from iterative diffusion-based restoration toward efficient one-step generation, a key challenge is to recover realistic and perceptually rich details within a single forward pass. To address this challenge, existing diffusion-based one-step SR methods [ 37 , 30 , 45 , 18 ] often employ score distillation or adversarial learning to enhance perceptual details. Score distillation approaches [ 33 , 37 , 10 ] typically rely on an additional teacher model and trainable LoRA branches, with the LoRA parameters optimized under diffusion-based supervision throughout training. Adversarial approaches [ 13 , 45 , 18 ] instead introduce an additional discriminator and may suffer from unstable optimization. Despite their effectiveness in improving perceptual quality, both paradigms require auxiliary trainable components and additional objectives, increasing the complexity of the training pipeline. This motivates a simpler alternative that optimizes only the one-step generator while effectively leveraging generative priors. The recently proposed Drifting Model [ 8 ] introduces an alternative to score distillation and adversarial learning for distributional generative optimization. It models the relation between source and target distributions in a pretrained feature space and constructs a drifting field guiding generated samples toward the target distribution. By operating on sample distributions without an additional discriminator or a separately optimized distillation branch, distribution drifting presents a potential alternative for one-step Real-ISR. Nevertheless, directly extending distribution drifting to one-step Real-ISR is non-trivial. First , the effectiveness of the drifting field depends strongly on the feature space used to measure sample relationships, while obtaining a suitable representation may require additional design for Real-ISR. Second , drifting at the image level constructs negative samples by excluding the current sample and therefore requires additional samples under the same condition. Such a requirement can be naturally satisfied in image generation conditioned on class labels or text prompts, where multiple images can share the same condition. In contrast, Real-ISR provides only one paired HQ target for each LQ input, leaving no additional sample for negative construction and thus preventing direct application of drifting at the image level. Third , Real-ISR requires both high perceptual quality and fidelity to the LQ input. Excessive drifting may encourage visually plausible textures that are inconsistent with the input, resulting in incorrect details and structural distortions. To address these challenges, we propose DriftSR , a one-step Real-ISR framework that adapts distribution drifting for perceptual detail enhancement. Inspired by Teacher-Feature Drifting (TFD) [ 50 ] , we employ the pretrained diffusion model as a frozen feature extractor and construct the drifting space using its intermediate representations. This design eliminates the need for an additional task-specific feature network while providing a representation space naturally aligned with the diffusion prior used by the generator. We further introduce Spatial Feature Drifting , which reformulates distribution modeling from the image level to the spatial feature level. By treating each spatial location as an individual sample, this formulation enables negative sample construction within each image and provides denser observations for modeling local texture distributions. To balance perceptual enhancement and input fidelity, we propose Structure-Modulated Guidance . Based on local structural consistency with the LQ input, this guidance adaptively modulates drifting supervision across spatial locations, thereby suppressing visually plausible but structurally inconsistent details. As shown in Figure 1 , these designs collectively enable DriftSR to leverage the pretrained diffusion prior for perceptual detail enhancement while preserving structural fidelity, with optimization restricted to the one-step generator. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose DriftSR, a one-step Real-ISR framework that introduces Spatial Feature Drifting to model distributions over spatial features and enhance perceptual details without additional trainable components. • We introduce Structure-Modulated Guidance to adaptively modulate drifting supervision based on local structural consistency with the LQ input, suppressing structural inconsistencies while preserving perceptually rich textures. • Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks demonstrate that our DriftSR achieves superior perceptual quality while maintaining efficient one-step inference. 2 Related work One-Step Diffusion-based Real-ISR. To reduce diffusion model inference costs in Real-ISR, recent studies have increasingly explored one-step generative models replacing iterative generation with a single forward pass [ 44 , 42 , 37 ] . These methods aim to substantially improve inference efficiency while preserving high perceptual restoration quality. Existing one-step Real-ISR methods [ 31 , 42 , 10 ] commonly adopt distribution or trajectory alignment objectives during training. Among them, distribution alignment is often achieved through score distillation, which constructs supervision from the score discrepancy between a frozen diffusion teacher and a trainable LoRA branch. Some methods further incorporate adversarial learning [ 45 , 18 , 52 ] to enhance perceptual quality, introducing an additional discriminator. Although these strategies achieve strong restoration performance, the auxiliary trainable components and additional objectives increase the complexity of the training pipeline. Therefore, we explore a simpler alternative that leverages pretrained diffusion priors to guide one-step Real-ISR, without auxiliary distillation branches or discriminators. Drifting Model. Drifting Model [ 8 ] introduces a new paradigm for one-step generation by moving distribution transport from inference to training. Unlike diffusion or flow-based models [ 23 , 12 , 3 ] that rely on iterative inference, the drifting model learns a one-step generator whose output distribution is progressively updated during training under a drifting field defined by a kernel. The drifting field attracts generated samples toward nearby target samples while repelling them from the current model distribution, thereby progressively aligning the two distributions. Since distribution transport is performed during training, inference requires only a single forward pass. The effectiveness of the drifting model depends on the representation space used to measure sample relationships [ 8 ] . For high-dimensional images, distances measured in pixel or latent space may not adequately capture perceptual and semantic similarity. The drifting model therefore uses pretrained representations to construct informative feature spaces, making the choice of feature space important for effective distribution alignment. 3 Method 3.1 Preliminary Drifting Model. Table 1 compares DriftSR with existing diffusion-based methods on three real-world datasets. The results yield three main observations. (1) DriftSR achieves the best overall performance on no-reference perceptual metrics across all three benchmarks. The advantage is particularly pronounced on the higher-resolution RealLQ250 dataset, indicating that DriftSR can more effectively leverage the rich generative priors of pretrained diffusion models to recover realistic perceptual details. (2) ResShift, CTMSR, and VOSR employ purely visual architectures without T2I diffusion priors. Although these methods achieve competitive performance on full-reference metrics such as PSNR and SSIM, they generally underperform DriftSR on no-reference perceptual metrics, suggesting limitations in recovering fine-grained high-frequency details. (3) Despite using the same SD2.1 prior, FiDeSR favors fidelity-oriented reconstruction, whereas DriftSR achieves substantially better perceptual performance, particularly on CLIPIQA and TOPIQ. Meanwhile, DriftSR does not consistently achieve the best scores on full-reference metrics, while maintaining strong perceptual performance. This observation is consistent with the recognized trade-off between fidelity and perceptual quality [ 4 , 9 ] . As richer perceptual details are recovered, full-reference metrics may not fully reflect perceptual quality and often favor smoother reconstructions [ 43 , 39 ] . Qualitative Comparisons. Figure 3 presents visual comparisons among different methods. In the first row, DriftSR reconstructs more natural and perceptually realistic textures, particularly for fine animal fur. Although ResShift, CTMSR, and VOSR achieve competitive PSNR and SSIM scores, their results exhibit noticeable over-smoothing. In the second row, DriftSR effectively suppresses degradation artifacts and recovers clearer structures with consistent colors, whereas other one-step methods show limited recovery of fine structures and fail to correct color distortions. These comparisons further demonstrate the stronger capability of DriftSR to leverage the generative prior. More visual comparisons are provided in the supplementary material . Complexity Comparisons. We further evaluate the computational efficiency of representative Real-ISR methods in Table 2 , considering inference steps, runtime, and model parameters. We measure inference time on the × 4 \times 4 SR task with 128 × 128 128\times 128 LQ inputs, applying bicubic upsampling before inference on a single NVIDIA 5880 GPU. DriftSR substantially reduces inference cost compared with multi-step methods. It is more than 72 times faster than StableSR, 35 times faster than DiT4SR, over 32 times faster than SeeSR, and 7 times faster than ResShift. Compared with existing one-step models, DriftSR matches OSEDiff in inference speed and is 6 times faster than CTMSR. Despite being slower than VOSR, TSD-SR, and FiDeSR, DriftSR achieves a favorable balance between computational efficiency and perceptual restoration quality. 4.3 Ablation Study Effectiveness of Drifting and SMG.
